content: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection affects approximately 260 million individuals globally and is responsible for around 900,000 deaths annually due to complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The highest prevalence of chronic HBV infection is observed in the Western Pacific and African regions. In 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) on viral hepatitis, aiming to eliminate HBV as a public health threat by 2030. This goal involves reducing the incidence of chronic HBV by 90% and its mortality by 65%. Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HBV is a significant contributor to the global burden of chronic HBV, as infection acquired early in life is more likely to become chronic. Furthermore, individuals who acquire HBV through MTCT may have a higher risk of developing chronic liver disease, including HCC, compared to those infected later in life through horizontal transmission. Preventing MTCT is therefore critical to achieving the WHO’s hepatitis elimination targets. Since 2009, WHO has recommended the administration of a timely birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine to all newborns within 24 hours of birth to prevent MTCT and early childhood transmission. While this intervention is generally effective in preventing MTCT in mothers with low HBV viral replication, 20–30% of infants born to mothers with high viral loads may still become infected despite timely vaccination. In high-income countries, pregnant women are routinely screened for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) to identify high-risk infants who may benefit from additional interventions, such as hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) at birth. In high-income settings, HBV DNA quantification has become a standard part of antenatal HBV testing to identify highly viremic women who may require antiviral therapy during pregnancy to further reduce the risk of MTCT. Nucleic acid testing (NAT), the current standard for measuring HBV DNA, is often inaccessible in these settings due to its high cost (ranging from $60 to $200 per test) and the need for sophisticated laboratory infrastructure and skilled personnel. As an alternative, HBeAg testing using laboratory-based immunoassays, such as enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA), or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) with lateral flow immunochromatographic assays, may offer a more affordable and accessible option. These tests are generally less expensive (ranging from $1 to $30 per test) and may be more feasible in resource-limited settings. To address the variability in defining high HBV DNA levels as a criterion for initiating antiviral therapy, this systematic review defined high HBV DNA levels as any value greater than or equal to 20,000 IU/mL. The primary objective of the review was to evaluate the performance of HBeAg testing as an alternative to HBV DNA testing for identifying pregnant women with chronic HBV who are eligible for antiviral therapy to prevent MTCT. Secondary objectives included assessing the sensitivity and specificity of HBeAg testing in predicting the risk of MTCT and evaluating the performance of different HBV DNA thresholds in predicting MTCT risk. The review included studies published between January 2000 and April 2019, with data extracted independently by two reviewers. The quality of included studies was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2) tool. Sensitivity and specificity estimates for HBeAg testing and HBV DNA thresholds were pooled when at least three studies were available. Heterogeneity across studies was evaluated using forest plots, summary scatter plots, and statistical models. The findings of this review are intended to inform WHO guidelines on the prevention of MTCT of HBV, particularly in resource-limited settings where access to NAT is restricted. By identifying cost-effective and accessible alternatives to HBV DNA testing, such as HBeAg testing, the review aims to support the global effort to eliminate HBV as a public health threat.
